source.notes: Symbol ids use the draft plan's module id (index). Fixtures call the same function through its import specifier, ms:default, which is what the JavaScript oracle resolves (package.json main ./index). Each symbol's callId names the fixture call id.

symbols.name: default
symbols.signature: ms(val: string | number, options?: { long?: any }): number | string | undefined
symbols.returns: typeof val === 'string' && val.length > 0: the parsed duration in milliseconds as a double, or undefined when the string is longer than 100 UTF-16 code units or does not match the grammar (options ignored). typeof val === 'number' && isFinite(val): a string, short form ('2s', '-3d', '0.5ms') or, when options.long is truthy, long form ('2 seconds', '1 day', '500 ms').

errors.when: val is not a non-empty string and not a finite number: '', undefined, null, booleans, arrays, objects, NaN, Infinity, -Infinity, boxed String or Number objects
errors.message: val is not a non-empty string or a valid number. val=<JSON.stringify(val)>

errors.when: val is a BigInt: JSON.stringify throws while building the message. JavaScript only; not in fixtures.
errors.message: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt

symbols.name: long
symbols.returns: Selects the long format when truthy (JavaScript truthiness: 1, 'yes', 'false' and [] are truthy; 0, '', null, false and a missing key are not). Read only when val is a finite number. options itself defaults through `options || {}`, so null and undefined mean {}.

leaks.description: Math.round rounds halves toward +infinity: ms(1500) is "2s", ms(-1500) is "-1s", ms(-2500) is "-2s". Go math.Round rounds away from zero (-2.5 gives -3). math.Floor(x+0.5) is also wrong: for odd integers in [2^52, 2^53) it adds one, while ms(3.891110078048109e+23) must be "4503599627370497d".

Long format picks the plural from the absolute value (|ms| >= 1.5 * unit) but rounds the signed value, so ms(-1500, {long: true}) is "-1 seconds" and ms(-90000, {long: true}) is "-1 minutes", while ms(-1499, {long: true}) is "-1 second". Under one second there is no pluralisation: "1 ms", "500 ms".

The unit is chosen from |ms| before rounding, so a value just below a unit boundary rounds up inside the smaller unit: ms(59999) is "60s", ms(3599999) is "60m", ms(86399999) is "24h". Days is the largest output unit: weeks and years are never printed (ms(31557600000) is "365d").

Numbers become text through JavaScript Number#toString (shortest round-trip digits, ECMAScript Number::toString). Below one second the input itself is printed: "0.5ms", "0.30000000000000004ms", "0.000001ms", but "9.99e-7ms", "1e-7ms" and "5e-324ms" (exponent form below 1e-6). Rounded counts print in full below 1e21 ("999999999999999900000d") and in exponent form from 1e21 ("1.0000000000000001e+21d", "1.1574074074074075e+292d"). The exponent has no zero padding and an explicit sign. Go strconv 'g' gives "1e-07" and switches to exponent form at other thresholds; 'f' never does.
Formatting -0 gives "0ms" and "0 ms" (JavaScript prints -0 as 0; Go strconv prints "-0"). Parsing "-0", "-0ms", "-0.0" or "-0.0d" returns -0, recorded as {"$float": "-0"}.

A non-empty string that is too long or does not match returns undefined (recorded as {"$undefined": true}). It is not NaN and not an error. The reference test 'should return NaN if invalid' passes only because isNaN(undefined) is true.

Parsed values are IEEE-754 doubles, parseFloat(number) * unit with s=1000, m=60000, h=3600000, d=86400000, w=604800000 and y=31557600000 (365.25 days). Results need not be integers: "1.15h" is 4139999.9999999995, "1.1d" is 95040000.00000001, ".5ms" is 0.5. parseFloat is correctly rounded on inputs up to 100 characters: "9007199254740993" is 9007199254740992, "1.50000000000000000001s" is 1500.

The regex /^(-?(?:\d+)?\.?\d+) *(milliseconds?|msecs?|ms|seconds?|secs?|s|minutes?|mins?|m|hours?|hrs?|h|days?|d|weeks?|w|years?|yrs?|y)?$/i is the whole input grammar: ASCII digits only; an optional leading '-' and no '+'; a leading '.' is allowed, a trailing '.' is not; no exponent, hex or digit separators; only U+0020 between number and unit, any count; trailing U+0020 is accepted after a unit-less number ("1 " is 1) but not after a unit ("1ms " is undefined); no leading whitespace; '$' is the end of input ("1m\n" is undefined). Units are case-insensitive under JavaScript's non-Unicode /i, which never folds a non-ASCII character to ASCII: "1ſ" and "1 weeK" are undefined. Go regexp (?i) folds ſ to s and K to k and accepts both.

A string longer than 100 UTF-16 code units returns undefined before matching ("9" x 100 is 1e100, "9" x 101 is undefined, "1" plus 99 spaces is 1). Only ASCII strings can match the grammar, so counting bytes, runes or UTF-16 units gives the same observable result.

The function dispatches on typeof val: a non-empty string is parsed and options are ignored; a finite number is formatted; anything else throws. The string branch never throws and the number branch never returns undefined. Boxed String and Number objects throw because typeof is 'object'.

options = options || {}; options.long is tested for truthiness. {long: 1}, {long: 'yes'}, {long: 'false'} and {long: []} give the long format; {long: 0}, {long: ''}, {long: null}, {long: false}, {} and null give the short format. Non-object options ('long', true) have no long property and give the short format. Extra keys are ignored.

Invalid input throws a plain Error (no subclass) whose message is 'val is not a non-empty string or a valid number. val=' + JSON.stringify(val): '' gives val="", undefined gives val=undefined, null, NaN, Infinity and -Infinity give val=null, arrays and objects give compact JSON (val={"a":1}). The reference tests only assert that a throw happens; the message is observable and recorded exactly. A BigInt argument instead throws TypeError from JSON.stringify (JavaScript only, not in fixtures).

Regex engine or a hand-written scanner, as long as the grammar leak holds.
The unreachable default branch of parse (index.js:100-101) and the String(str) coercion inside parse (only strings reach it).
